To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the ability of genetically encoded calcium indicators to report neuronal activity has been greatly improved by recent advances in indicator design and delivery, and (2) these advances have enabled the development of new methods for studying neural circuits in behaving rodents.

(1) we developed a new method for imaging neuronal activity in awake mice using a miniature microscope and (2) we found that neurons in the primary auditory cortex of awake mice exhibit a wide range of firing rates and response latencies to auditory stimuli, and that these properties are correlated with the spatial location of neurons within the cortex.

(i) calcium imaging in awake, behaving rodents can provide a wealth of information about the neural correlates of task-dependent behavior; (ii) the development of new behavioral paradigims, head-fixed and freely moving animals, and new imaging technologies has enabled these studies; (iii) the combination of these methods with viral-mediated and transgenic tools has enabled the study of neural circuits underlying behavior in the mammalain cortex.
